sections.heading: What is the Cyclic Sort Pattern?
sections.content: Cyclic Sort works on arrays that contain numbers in a known range, usually 1 to n or 0 to n. Because each value has a natural home index (value 1 belongs at index 0, value 2 at index 1, and so on), you can place every number directly in its correct position by swapping. Once placed, any index that holds the wrong number reveals a missing, duplicate or misplaced value. It sorts in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: The array has numbers in the range 1..n or 0..n
You need to find missing numbers
You need to find duplicate numbers
You need the first missing positive
The problem demands O(n) time and O(1) space (no HashSet, no sorting)
You are allowed to modify the input array
Keywords: missing, duplicate, corrupt pair, range 1 to n, in place

rows.example: n has no slot, ignore it during placement

sections.heading: The Intuition
sections.content: Look at the element at index i. If it is not in its home index, swap it with whatever sits at its home. Repeat on index i until the element at i is either home or a duplicate of the one already home. Then move to i + 1. Every swap places at least one number permanently, so there are at most n swaps in total. Even though there is a loop inside a loop, the total time is O(n).

Why Compare nums[i] with nums[correct]
sections.content: Checking nums[i] != nums[correct] (the values) instead of i != correct (the positions) is what protects you from infinite loops when duplicates exist. If the target slot already holds the same value, a swap would change nothing, so you must advance i.

rows.key_idea: Swap each value to index value - 1
Home index is the value itself, skip n
Indexes with wrong value are missing
Duplicate is found when its home is taken
Wrong value at an index is the duplicate
One misplaced index gives both answers

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Comparing i with the home index instead of comparing nums[i] with nums[correct], which creates infinite loops with duplicates
Incrementing i after every swap (you must recheck the new value at i)
Index out of bounds: forgetting the range guard when values can be 0, negative or larger than n
Using home index = value when values start at 1 (or the other way around)
Using cyclic sort when the input must not be modified
Forgetting that the missing number in 0..n may be n itself
Returning index instead of index + 1 when values are 1-based

sections.heading: Why It Is O(n) and Not O(n²)
sections.content: The inner swaps look like a nested loop, but each swap puts one value into its final home, and a placed value is never moved again. There can be at most n such placements, and i only advances when no swap is needed. So the total number of steps is bounded by about 2n.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Use cyclic sort when numbers are in the range 1..n or 0..n
Home index is value - 1 for 1-based values and value for 0-based values
Swap while the value at i is not home and the target is not already the same value
After placement, indexes holding the wrong value reveal missing and duplicate numbers
Guard against out-of-range values before using them as an index
The total time is O(n) because every swap places a value permanently
